decisionSource: The Wyoming Legislative Service Office's own publication of Titles 6, 7, 12, 14 and 21 of the Wyoming Statutes, and its own publication of the enrolled acts that created and amended W.S. 7-13-1501, W.S. 7-13-1502 and W.S. 6-4-305. Read against the integrated Wyoming legal-design memo, the normalized track registry, the packet-set manifests and the authoritative blocker ledger.
whatThisDocumentIs: The decision record that answers the two substantive reads blocking the Wyoming misdemeanour track: what W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii) actually defines as a status offence, on which the one-year and five-year clocks turn, and whether an expungement under W.S. 7-13-1501 restores any right when W.S. 7-13-1502(m) expressly does and 7-13-1501 appears not to. It amends no memo, regenerates no registry, implements nothing and asserts no counsel approval.

scopeOfThisJob.trackTouched: None. This record adjudicates two questions on wy_misd_1501, one of which bears on wy_fel_1502 by comparison, and writes only itself.
scopeOfThisJob.questionsExpresslyNotReached: Currency and the session sweeps, the original enactment dates, whether anything reaches a completed felony deferral, and the Lynch citation all belong to rcap-wy-governing-mechanism-and-currency-reconciliation and are not re-decided here; where that record's findings are needed they are cited to it and to the same primary sources. The twenty-three-county local-template survey is untouched and remains a build blocker on all three tracks. Nothing here reaches wy_nc_1401's own questions.

questionsPresented: What does Wyo. Stat. § 7-1-107(b)(iii) define as a status offence, and which common Wyoming charges fall inside it? The one-year and five-year clocks in § 7-13-1501(a)(i) turn entirely on this.
Does an expungement under § 7-13-1501 restore any right, given that § 7-13-1502(m) carries an express restoration provision and § 7-13-1501 does not appear to?
methodNote: Both questions are answered by reading the enacted text rather than by reasoning from the shape of the statutes. For the first, the definition was read in its own section, every place in the Wyoming code that uses the phrase was located, and the offences that could produce a misdemeanour conviction for conduct lawful for an adult were enumerated from Titles 6, 12, 14 and 21 rather than guessed at from the concept. For the second, the assignment forbids curing the asymmetry by reading § 7-13-1502(m) across into § 7-13-1501, so the two sections were read as drafted and then traced back through their enacting and amending acts to see whether the difference is an accident or a decision. It is a decision, and the act that made it names itself.

controllingSources.citation: Wyo. Stat. § 7-1-107(b)(iii), Detention of juvenile offenders — definitions
controllingSources.verbatimText: "Status offense" means an offense which, if committed by an adult, would not constitute an act punishable as a criminal offense by the laws of this state or a violation of a municipal ordinance, but does not include a violation of W.S. 12-6-101(b) or (c) or any similar municipal ordinance;

(a)(i) At least five (5) years have passed for nonstatus offenses and at least one (1) year has passed for status offenses as defined by W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii) since the expiration of the terms of sentence imposed by the court, including any periods of probation or the completion of any program ordered by the court;
controllingSources.definitionsCarried: (m)(i) "Expungement" means as defined in W.S. 7-13-1401(j)(i); (m)(ii) "Misdemeanor" means as defined by W.S. 6-10-101; (m)(iii) "Record" means as defined in W.S. 7-13-1401(j)(ii); (m)(iv) "Health care provider" …

controllingSources.citation: Wyo. Stat. § 6-4-305, Dissemination or possession of a nude image of a minor by a minor
controllingSources.verbatimText: (e) A minor convicted of violating subsection (b) of this section is guilty of a status offense as defined in W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii) and may be fined not more than two hundred fifty dollars ($250.00).
controllingSources.enactedBy: 2017 House Bill 0238, Session Laws of Wyoming 2017 ch. 190, effective 2017-07-01, "W.S. 6-4-305 is created to read".
controllingSources.operativeFinding: This is the only place in the Wyoming code where the legislature attaches the label "status offense as defined in W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii)" to a specific offence. Subsection (b) reaches a minor who knowingly disseminates a nude image of himself, or possesses a nude image of another minor at least eleven years of age subject to the inadvertent-possession exception. Subsections (c) and (d) are ordinary misdemeanours by (f) and are not status offences.

Subsection (b) reads in the codification "Repealed By Laws 2010, Ch. 6, § 2." Subsection (c) is live and carries the whole under-21 prohibition: purchasing or attempting to purchase, soliciting another to purchase, possessing, consuming ethyl alcohol, having a measurable alcohol concentration, entering or remaining in designated off-premise sales areas unaccompanied, and dispensing or selling.

controllingSources.verbatimText: No conviction under this section, whether by guilty plea, adjudication of guilt or forfeiture of bond shall be reported by the court to any law enforcement agency. Upon payment of the fine imposed by subsection (b) of this section, a criminal conviction under this section shall be expunged by operation of law from all records of the court six (6) months after the entry of conviction. For any person whose record of conviction was expunged under this subsection, the conviction is deemed not to have occurred and the individual may reply accordingly upon any inquiry in the matter. No expungement under this subsection shall be considered for purposes of any other law providing for expungement.

sourcesExpresslyNotRelieduponAsProof: No commercial code compilation, annotation, practitioner guide, law-firm page or reentry-policy database was used to establish any text or date.
No county or municipal ordinance was read. Where the answer turns on municipal ordinances it is recorded as unresolved rather than assumed in either direction.
No inference is drawn from the absence of a search result. The enumeration of candidate offences is described so it can be falsified.

statusOffence.1_whatTheDefinitionSays: A status offence is conduct that is an offence only because of who the actor is. The test is counterfactual and it is stated in the negative: an offence which, if committed by an adult, would not be punishable as a criminal offence under state law or as a municipal ordinance violation. The definition then carves one thing back out — a violation of W.S. 12-6-101(b) or (c) or any similar municipal ordinance is never a status offence, however it would look to an adult.

2_whereTheDefinitionLives.finding: In W.S. 7-1-107, Detention of juvenile offenders, and its subsection (b) opens "As used in W.S. 7-1-107 and 7-1-108:" — a scoping clause naming two sections, neither of which is an expungement section.
2_whereTheDefinitionLives.doesThatDefeatTheIncorporation: No. W.S. 7-13-1501(a)(i) does not rely on the definition applying of its own force; it cross-references it by section, subsection and paragraph — "status offenses as defined by W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii)" — which is how a scoped definition is borrowed. The reference is unambiguous and there is only one candidate.
2_whereTheDefinitionLives.whyItIsRecordedAnyway: Because a reader who follows the cross-reference lands in a juvenile-detention statute and may reasonably wonder whether the borrowing carries the juvenile context with it. It does not: 7-13-1501 applies to persons, not to minors, and the borrowed text is a definition rather than a scope. Two other sections of the code carry the same definition in nearly identical words for their own acts — W.S. 14-6-201(a)(xxiii) and W.S. 14-6-402(a)(xx), the latter without the "or any similar municipal ordinance" tail — and neither is the one 7-13-1501 points at. The difference between them is immaterial to any outcome here, but a normalizer reaching for a Title 14 definition would be reaching for the wrong one.

3_aDefectInTheCarveOut.finding: The carve-out excludes "a violation of W.S. 12-6-101(b) or (c)", and W.S. 12-6-101(b) was repealed by Laws 2010, ch. 6, § 2. Half the carve-out points at nothing.
3_aDefectInTheCarveOut.effect: None on any outcome. Subsection (c) carries the entire under-21 prohibition — purchase, attempted purchase, solicitation, possession, consumption of ethyl alcohol, measurable alcohol concentration, presence in designated off-premise sales areas unaccompanied, and dispensing or selling — so nothing escapes the carve-out through the repealed subsection.
3_aDefectInTheCarveOut.whyRecorded: So that no one reads (b) as a live carve-out with separate content, and so that a future revisor's amendment to 7-1-107(b)(iii) is recognised as housekeeping rather than as a change of scope.

expresslyLabelledByStatute.offence: W.S. 6-4-305(b) — a minor who knowingly disseminates a nude image of himself, or possesses a nude image of another minor at least eleven years of age, subject to the inadvertent-possession exception.
expresslyLabelledByStatute.basis: W.S. 6-4-305(e) says so in terms: such a minor "is guilty of a status offense as defined in W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii)". This is the only express legislative identification of a status offence anywhere in the Wyoming code, and it uses the same cross-reference 7-13-1501(a)(i) uses.
expresslyLabelledByStatute.consequence: A conviction under 6-4-305(b) carries the one-year clock. A conviction under 6-4-305(c) or (d) does not: subsection (f) makes those ordinary misdemeanours, so they carry five years.

insideTheDefinitionButNeverReaching1501.offences: W.S. 14-3-304, purchase or attempted purchase of nicotine products by a person under twenty-one, and W.S. 14-3-305, possession or use of nicotine products by a person under twenty-one. Both are misdemeanours, both are lawful for an adult, and neither is carved out, so both satisfy the definition.
insideTheDefinitionButNeverReaching1501.whyTheyNeverReach1501: Each section expunges itself. W.S. 14-3-304(d) and 14-3-305(e) provide that the court shall not report the conviction to any law enforcement agency and that, on payment of the fine, the conviction "shall be expunged by operation of law from all records of the court six (6) months after the entry of conviction", after which "the conviction is deemed not to have occurred and the individual may reply accordingly upon any inquiry". A participant with such a conviction has nothing left to petition about.
insideTheDefinitionButNeverReaching1501.andItCostsThemNothing: Each subsection ends "No expungement under this subsection shall be considered for purposes of any other law providing for expungement." So an automatic nicotine expungement does not consume the once-in-a-lifetime allowance W.S. 7-13-1501(k) imposes. That is a participant-facing fact worth stating rather than leaving to inference.

outsideTheSectionAltogether.conduct: Habitual truancy as defined in W.S. 21-4-101(a)(ii), running away from home, habitually disobeying the reasonable and lawful demands of a parent, guardian, custodian or other proper authority, and being ungovernable and beyond control.
outsideTheSectionAltogether.why: These are the Child in Need of Supervision grounds in W.S. 14-6-402(a)(iv), and that paragraph expressly includes "any child … who has committed a status offense". They are dealt with in the juvenile court by adjudication. W.S. 7-13-1501(a) reaches only "A person who has pled guilty or nolo contendere to or been convicted of a misdemeanor", and a CHINS adjudication is none of those three things. So the most commonly imagined status offences cannot reach the misdemeanour expungement track at all, whichever clock would apply.
outsideTheSectionAltogether.careRequired: This is the single most likely mis-screen on this track. A participant who says "I had a truancy case as a kid" is describing a juvenile matter that 7-13-1501 does not reach, and the packet must not route them into the one-year branch on the strength of the word.

expresslyExcluded.offence: W.S. 12-6-101(c), the under-twenty-one alcohol offences, and any similar municipal ordinance.
expresslyExcluded.consequence: Five years, not one. This is the most consequential single answer in this record, because under-twenty-one alcohol is the most common Wyoming charge a participant would expect to be treated as a youthful status matter, and the legislature put it outside the definition in terms.

notResolved.question: Municipal-ordinance-only offences that apply to minors alone, of which a curfew ordinance is the obvious example.
notResolved.twoStepProblem: Such conduct satisfies the status-offence definition, because an adult doing it violates neither a state criminal law nor a municipal ordinance. But 7-13-1501 reaches a "misdemeanor" as W.S. 6-10-101 defines it, and 6-10-101 defines felony and misdemeanour by reference to "crimes" punishable by imprisonment — it does not say whether a municipal ordinance violation is a crime for that purpose. Whether a municipal ordinance conviction is expungeable under 7-13-1501 at all is therefore a prior question to the clock, and it is not answered here.
notResolved.whyNotAnswered: It would take reading municipal ordinances and the law of municipal court jurisdiction, neither of which this assignment reaches, and guessing it would be inventing an eligibility rule.

5_theDesignConsequence.theOneYearBranchIsRealButNarrow: It has exactly one statutorily identified occupant that can produce a live misdemeanour conviction needing expungement: W.S. 6-4-305(b). Everything else that looks like a status offence is either automatically expunged already, outside the section because it is a juvenile adjudication, or expressly carved out.
5_theDesignConsequence.soTheDefaultIsFiveYears: For any Wyoming misdemeanour a participant is likely to bring, the clock is five years from the expiration of the terms of sentence including any period of probation and the completion of any court-ordered programme. The one-year branch is the exception and must be justified from the charging section, never from the participant's description of themselves as having been young at the time.
5_theDesignConsequence.whatDrivesTheBranch: The Revised Statutes section the person was convicted under, taken from the court record. That is a determinate input a packet can ask for and a participant can supply from their own judgment and sentence.
5_theDesignConsequence.whatMustNotDriveIt: The participant's age at the time of the offence, the fact that the case was in juvenile court, the word "status" appearing in their recollection, or the offence merely being minor. None of those is the statutory test.
5_theDesignConsequence.buildBlockerStatus: Answered. The clock is determinable from the charging section for every offence the statute reaches, so the waiting period is no longer an undetermined design element on wy_misd_1501.

1_whatSection1501Does.finding: Two things, and only two. It expunges the record — which W.S. 7-13-1501(m)(i) defines by adopting W.S. 7-13-1401(j)(i), namely the classification of the record held in the state central repository at the division of criminal investigation so that it is not available for dissemination other than to criminal justice agencies for criminal justice purposes — and under 7-13-1501(g) the court places its own files under seal, available for inspection only by order of that court.
1_whatSection1501Does.whatItIsNot: It is not destruction. The record continues to exist and continues to be available to criminal justice agencies of any state and to federal criminal justice agencies. The definition expressly does not reach investigatory files of any local, state or federal criminal justice agency where those files are used solely for criminal justice purposes.
1_whatSection1501Does.restoresNothingByItsOwnTerms: Section 7-13-1501 was read in full, subsections (a) through (m). There is no restoration provision. Its subsection (m) is the definitions subsection, which is what makes the comparison with 7-13-1502(m) so easy to misread — the two sections use the same letter for different things.

restoration.2_whatSection1502Does: Everything 7-13-1501 does, plus subsection (m): "An expungement of records pursuant to this section shall restore any rights removed as a result of the conviction for which the expungement has been granted." The section's own heading carries "restoration of rights" and has since it was enacted.

3_isTheAsymmetryDeliberate.answer: Yes, and it is traceable to a specific act whose own title says what it did.
theHistory: 2004 Senate File 0064, ch. 69, effective 2004-07-01, created W.S. 7-13-1501 together with Article 15. As enacted, subsection (a) let a person petition "for an expungement of the records of conviction for the purposes of restoring any firearm rights lost". Restoration was not merely available under the section; it was the section's stated and only purpose, and the catch title of the act was "Restoration of firearm rights-expungement". The waiting period was one year for every qualifying misdemeanour.

2009 House Bill 0106, ch. 67, effective 2009-02-26, amended (a)(intro), (a)(i), (a)(ii) and (k). Its own title is "AN ACT relating to criminal procedure; amending the purposes for which an expungement under W.S. 7-13-1501 may be used". After it, the purpose clause is gone from (a); subsection (k), which had read "An expungement granted pursuant to this section shall only be used for the purposes of restoring firearm rights that have been lost to persons convicted of misdemeanors" together with a penalty-enhancement savings sentence, carries only the once-in-a-lifetime rule that is there today; and the one-year clock became five years.

2011 Senate File 0088, ch. 69, effective 2011-07-01, created W.S. 7-13-1502 as a new section, two years later and in a separate act. It carried "restoration of rights" in its heading and the subsection (m) restoration provision from the first day.
2015 Senate File 0018, ch. 164, effective 2015-07-01, inserted the status-offence split into 7-13-1501(a)(i) and repealed (a)(ii).

2018 House Bill 0157, ch. 80, effective 2018-07-01, struck the enumerated misdemeanour list from (a)(intro) so the section reaches any misdemeanour, added the health-care-provider bar at (a)(iv) and its definition at (m)(iv), and added "exceptions" to the section heading. No restoration provision was added then either, when the section stopped being a firearm-rights route and became a general one.
3_isTheAsymmetryDeliberate.howTheAttributionWasMade: By delta rather than by formatting. The enrolled text of 2009 ch. 67 prints both the purpose clause and the new (k) sentence, and both the one-year and the five-year clock, because struck and inserted language sit side by side once the formatting is lost. The section as codified carries the five-year clock, no purpose clause in (a), and only the once-in-a-lifetime sentence in (k). Each of the three later acts that amended (a)(intro) — 2014 ch. 13, 2015 ch. 164 and 2018 ch. 80 — prints (a)(intro) without a purpose clause. The struck material in 2009 is therefore the purpose clause and the first two sentences of (k), which is exactly what that act's own title describes.
3_isTheAsymmetryDeliberate.whyItMatters: The legislature did not forget to put restoration in 7-13-1501. It put restoration in, then took it out, and later wrote it into a different section. Reading 7-13-1502(m) across into 7-13-1501 would restore by construction the very thing an act titled "amending the purposes for which an expungement under W.S. 7-13-1501 may be used" repealed.

restoration.4_doNotCrossRead: The assignment forbids resolving the asymmetry by reading 7-13-1502(m) across, and the history is why the prohibition is right rather than merely cautious. The two sections were enacted seven years apart in unrelated acts, they are differently drafted throughout — different fee, different objection window, different exclusions, different heading — and the one that lacks restoration lost it by amendment. Nothing in this record supports the cross-read and nothing in it should be cited for one.

5_aThirdAsymmetryTheMemoDidNotCarry.finding: W.S. 7-13-1401(f) provides that a person who has received an order of expungement "under this section" may respond to any inquiry as though the arrest or charge did not occur, unless otherwise provided by law. Neither 7-13-1501 nor 7-13-1502 has an equivalent provision, and 1401(f) is confined to its own section by its own words.
5_aThirdAsymmetryTheMemoDidNotCarry.consequence: On both conviction routes the packet may say what the order does to the division of criminal investigation record and to the court file, and may not tell the participant they are entitled to answer an inquiry as though the conviction did not occur. That entitlement exists on the non-conviction route and, by their own terms, on the two nicotine sections. It does not exist on 7-13-1501 or 7-13-1502.

mayState: That the court will place its files under seal, available for inspection only by order of that court.

That the division of criminal investigation record is reclassified so it is not disseminated other than to criminal justice agencies of any state or federal criminal justice agencies, for criminal justice purposes only.
That the section reaches only the records it defines, and does not reach investigatory files held by any criminal justice agency for criminal justice purposes.
That relief is discretionary: the court must find both eligibility and that the petitioner does not represent a substantial danger to himself, any identifiable victim or society.
mustNotState: That any right is restored. Section 7-13-1501 restores none by its own terms and the legislature removed the provision that once did.

That firearm rights are restored. That is the specific promise the section was created to make in 2004 and the specific promise the 2009 act removed, and it is the promise a participant is most likely to be seeking.
That the participant may answer an inquiry as though the conviction did not occur.
That the record is destroyed, erased or gone.
6_whatMayBePromisedOnTheMisdemeanourTrac.federalBoundary: Whether any federal consequence follows from a Wyoming expungement is outside this record and is not asserted in either direction. Nothing here should be read as advice about federal firearms law, and a participant asking about it is a stop condition rather than a copy problem.

restoration.7_effectOnTheFelonyTrack: None by way of change. Section 7-13-1502(m) means what it says and wy_fel_1502 may state that an expungement under that section restores any rights removed as a result of the expunged conviction. What this record adds is the reason the two tracks may not share that sentence, so that a later editor does not harmonise the copy and make the misdemeanour packet promise something the statute does not.

The definition is quoted, the one expressly labelled occupant is W.S. 6-4-305(b), under-twenty-one alcohol is expressly carved out and takes five years, nicotine offences are expunged by operation of law and never reach the section, and CHINS conduct is a juvenile adjudication outside the section entirely.

items.recorded: Two entries, one for a non-status misdemeanour at five years and one for a status offence as defined by W.S. 7-1-107(b)(iii) at one year.
items.correct: Both durations are right and neither changes. What should be added is the condition text that makes the branch determinable: that a status offence is one that would not be an offence for an adult, that under-twenty-one alcohol under W.S. 12-6-101(c) is expressly excluded and takes five years, and that the branch is decided from the Revised Statutes section of conviction rather than from the participant's age.

Add that a juvenile Child in Need of Supervision adjudication for truancy, running away, disobedience or ungovernability is not a plea or conviction of a misdemeanour and is outside W.S. 7-13-1501; and add a stop condition for a municipal-ordinance-only conviction, because whether such a conviction is a "misdemeanor" as W.S. 6-10-101 defines it for 7-13-1501(m)(ii) is unresolved.

items.recorded: nonblocking_research_note: does an expungement under 7-13-1501 restore any rights?
items.correct: Retire against this record with the answer: no right is restored, and the omission is deliberate and traceable to 2009 ch. 67.

Record, as a packet_instruction, that the misdemeanour packet may not promise restoration of any right — firearm rights in particular — and may not promise an entitlement to answer an inquiry as though the conviction did not occur, because W.S. 7-13-1401(f) is confined to its own section.

terminalDispositionDetail.why: The narrowest accurate result. It is not a readiness statement: the local-template build blocker is untouched and no Wyoming track becomes generatable. It is not a cross-read: the restoration answer is grounded in the drafting history of the two sections rather than in their similarity. And it does not overstate the status-offence answer — the definition is now determinable for every offence the section reaches, and the one class it cannot yet resolve, municipal-ordinance-only offences, is recorded as a new build blocker rather than papered over.
terminalDispositionDetail.howTheEnumerationWasDone: By reading the offences rather than the concept. Every candidate that could produce a misdemeanour conviction for conduct lawful for an adult was located in Titles 6, 12, 14 and 21 and then classified: expressly labelled, inside but self-expunging, expressly carved out, outside the section because it is a juvenile adjudication, or unresolved because it turns on municipal law.
